questions.question_text: A curve has gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6\sin 3x$ and passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\, 1\right)$. Find the equation of the curve.

options.why: Evaluated $\cos\pi$ as $1$ instead of $-1$ when solving for $C$.
Dropped the minus sign from $\int\sin x\,dx$ and then solved for $C$ consistently with that primitive.
Dropped the minus sign in the primitive but kept the constant found from the correct primitive.

questions.solution_text:
$y = \int 6\sin 3x\,dx$
$= -\dfrac{6}{3}\cos 3x + C$
$= -2\cos 3x + C$
Substitute $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $y = 1$.
$1 = -2\cos\pi + C$
$1 = 2 + C$
$C = -1$
$y = -2\cos 3x - 1$

questions.question_text: Find $\int\dfrac{1}{k}\sec^{2}(kx + m)\,dx$, where $k$ and $m$ are constants and $k \ne 0$.

options.why: Kept only the $\dfrac{1}{k}$ already in the integrand and forgot to divide again by the coefficient $k$.
Cancelled the $\dfrac{1}{k}$ in the integrand against the $k$ from the chain rule instead of dividing by $k$ a second time.
Multiplied by the coefficient $k$ instead of dividing by it, cancelling the $\dfrac{1}{k}$ the wrong way.

questions.solution_text:
$a = k$, so the primitive of $\sec^{2}(kx + m)$ is $\dfrac{1}{k}\tan(kx + m)$.
$\int\dfrac{1}{k}\sec^{2}(kx + m)\,dx$
$= \dfrac{1}{k} \times \dfrac{1}{k}\tan(kx + m) + C$
$= \dfrac{1}{k^{2}}\tan(kx + m) + C$
